newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS - Brazil's Banespa closer to sell-off.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Brazil's Banespa closer to sell-off.

text.p: Sao Paulo's troubled state bank Banespa was pushed a giant step closer to the auction block Wednesday when the state agreed to hand over control of the bank to the federal government under a major debt rescheduling deal.
Sao Paulo state Governor Mario Covas and federal officials agreed that the state's 51 percent stake in Banespa would be sold to Brasilia for a price to be determined after one year.
While in federal hands for one year, Banespa will be run by an independent manager who will be hired in a bidding process, said Finance Ministry Executive Secretary Pedro Parente.
Banespa has been under Central Bank management since December 1994 due to financial problems stemming from Sao Paulo state's huge 20.6 billion real ($19.9 billion) debt to the bank.
Although Sao Paulo retains the right to buy back Banespa, Brazil's largest state bank, Covas made it clear that the state was not in financial shape to do so.
"I don't think it's possible to recover the bank," Covas told reporters during a news conference to announce the deal.
Most observers say Brasilia eventually intends to privatize the bank, but officials have so far remained mum about their plans.
"I like to cross the bridge when I get to it. We haven't gotten there yet," Finance Minister Pedro Malan told reporters who questioned him about the bank's fate.

The sale of Sao Paulo's 51 percent stake in Banespa to Brasilia is part of an overall refinancing package aimed at rescheduling a big chunk of Sao Paulo's massive debt -- the largest of all Brazilian states, totaling more than 60 billion reais.

Some analysts were critical of the deal, which still needs approval from federal and state lawmakers. They noted it represented a continuation of a long tradition of Brazilian states handing off financial disasters to Brasilia.
But others said the deal at least settles the lingering Banespa problem for now and points policy-makers charged with finding an ultimate solution for the bank in the right direction.

"Before we had a situation that was undefined. Today, a solution was defined that is most likely going to end in the privatization of Banespa and with Sao Paulo state government accounts in order," Dany Rappaport, chief economist for MCM Consultores in Brazil.
The debt to be refinanced under the new deal totals 36.5 billion reais, but officials said the figure could change depending on how quickly federal and state lawmakers approved the plan.
Under the deal, the debt would be refinanced over a 30-year period at an interest rate of six percent plus inflation.

In addition, the deal requires Sao Paulo state to pay off another 7.4 billion reais of its debt through asset sales. The assets, which may include real estate holdings and state firms already slated for privatization, will be selected by the Sao Paulo state government and Brazil's National Development Bank (BNDES).

Sao Paulo debt covered under the plan is owed to state banks Banespa and Nossa Caixa Nosso Banco and to holders of government securities. The debt not covered by the deal was refinanced at an earlier date and is not considered a problem by the government.
The terms of the package are similar to deals reached in September with Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul states for 8.6 billion reais and 6.0 billion reais respectively.
